edition.sessionCovered: Tue, Nov 10 (Hot CPI sinks gold 2.6% to $4,032 · WASDE cuts corn yield to 179.6 · Brent $91.49 · BTC $73,500)
edition.stripNote: Wed 11 Nov. October CPI came in hot — 0.4% MoM headline vs 0.3% consensus and 0.3% core vs 0.2% — sending gold crashing 2.6% to $4,032, its worst single-day drop in months, and pushing Treasury yields to 4.68%. Fed Governor Waller said a 50bp hike 'should be considered' at the December meeting, lifting odds to roughly 15%. Brent settled at $91.49, down 1.2%, as Iran deal talks expanded to nuclear dimensions with a 3.67% enrichment cap and IAEA inspections on the table. Trump called the war 'effectively over.' The WASDE surprised with a bullish corn yield cut to 179.6 bu/acre from 181.2, lifting corn 1.35% to 449¢ and soybeans 2.5% to 1,225¢. BTC slipped to $73,500 amid $1.3 billion in weekly ETF outflows. S&P 7,521 (−0.38%), Dow 52,232 (−0.30%), Nasdaq 25,066 (−0.74%). China's Nov 27 export-control deadline now 16 days away.

overview: October CPI came in hotter than expected on Tuesday, reshaping the rates outlook and hammering gold. Headline CPI rose 0.4% month-over-month against a 0.3% consensus, while core printed 0.3% versus the expected 0.2%. The BLS again did not publish 12-month changes because October 2025 data was not collected during last year's government shutdown, but the Cleveland Fed's nowcast implies an annual rate above 3.7%. The Treasury 10-year yield jumped to 4.68%, its highest since early October, and Fed Governor Waller said a 50-basis-point hike 'should be considered' at the December 8–9 FOMC meeting — lifting the probability of a double hike to roughly 15%. Gold crashed 2.6% to $4,032 per ounce, its worst single-day decline in months, as higher yields raised the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. Silver fell 3.9% to $51.32. Oil continued its descent: Brent settled at $91.49, down 1.2%, as Iran deal talks expanded dramatically to include nuclear dimensions — a 3.67% uranium enrichment cap, IAEA inspections and up to $9 billion in sanctions relief. President Trump told reporters the war is 'effectively over.' WTI fell to $86.04. US equities retreated modestly as the CPI print overrode the midterm relief: the S&P 500 fell 0.38% to 7,521, the Dow slipped 0.30% to 52,232 and the Nasdaq dropped 0.74% to 25,066.

The USDA's November WASDE report delivered a bullish surprise for grains. US corn yield was cut to 179.6 bushels per acre from 181.2, below the lowest analyst estimate, and ending stocks were trimmed deeper than expected. December corn rallied 1.35% to settle at 449¢ per bushel. Soybeans surged 2.51% to 1,225¢ as the report also tightened the soybean balance sheet. Wheat gained 0.80% to 593¢, supported by the broader grains bid and continued tightness in Black Sea export corridors. Bitcoin slid to approximately $73,500, down 0.8%, as spot ETF outflows reached $1.3 billion for a second consecutive week and the Fear and Greed Index fell to 30. Ethereum dropped to $2,040. Base metals declined broadly on the higher-yield environment: copper fell 1.19% to $6.25 per pound ($13,780 per tonne LME), nickel dropped 1.26% to $16,085, and zinc fell 0.72% to $3,709. Newcastle coal slid 2% to $138 per tonne. Tin edged up 0.24% to $46,313 on continued supply tightness. Cocoa extended its slide toward $4,700 per tonne, near a four-month low, on rising ICE warehouse inventories. China's November 27 deadline to re-impose export controls on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials is now 16 days away.

watchItems.title: Hot CPI resets the rate outlook: Waller floats a 50bp December hike
watchItems.text: October CPI delivered a hawkish surprise — 0.4% MoM headline versus 0.3% consensus and 0.3% core versus 0.2%. The BLS still cannot publish 12-month rates due to the October 2025 shutdown gap, but the Cleveland Fed nowcast implies above 3.7% annual. The 10-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.68%, its highest since early October. Fed Governor Waller said a 50-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC meeting 'should be considered,' lifting the implied probability to roughly 15%. Markets had been pricing a single 25bp move as near certain. Gold absorbed the heaviest blow, crashing 2.6% to $4,032, while equities retreated modestly. The hot print validates the Fed's hawkish tilt and raises the bar for any dovish pivot. The next key data point is the November employment report on December 5.

watchItems.title: WASDE bullish surprise: corn yield cut below all estimates
watchItems.text: The USDA's November WASDE report surprised the market by cutting the US corn yield forecast to 179.6 bushels per acre from 181.2 in October, below the lowest analyst estimate. US corn ending stocks were trimmed deeper than expected, tightening the 2026/27 balance sheet. December corn rallied 1.35% to 449¢ per bushel. The soybean balance sheet was also tightened, sending January soybeans up 2.51% to 1,225¢ per bushel. Wheat gained 0.80% to 593¢. The yield cut reflects late-season dryness in portions of the western Corn Belt. Managed money was positioned net short going into the report, amplifying the upside reaction. The bullish WASDE offsets some of the broader risk-off mood created by the hot CPI print.

watchItems.title: Iran deal expands to nuclear dimensions — Trump says war 'effectively over'
watchItems.text: Iran deal talks expanded dramatically on Tuesday beyond the original Hormuz reopening proposal. The framework now includes a 3.67% uranium enrichment cap, IAEA inspections of Iranian facilities and up to $9 billion in sanctions relief — significantly broader than Monday's $8 billion Hormuz-only proposal. President Trump told reporters the war is 'effectively over,' though cabinet members remain divided. Brent fell 1.2% to $91.49 as the market priced rising peace odds, extending the 16% weekly decline. However, four strait attacks occurred November 1–3 and the Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Aramco's Riyadh offices. Eurasia Group's peace probability remains at just 10%. Any deal collapse would trigger a violent snap-back in oil — physical Gulf supply remains tight, with Murban crude near $99.

watchItems.title: China's Nov 27 export-control deadline: 16 days and counting
watchItems.text: China's suspension of its prohibition on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard material exports to the US expires November 27 — now 16 days away. The suspension, announced November 9, 2025 as part of the Busan truce, has not restored meaningful export volumes. Gallium remains near $2,100 per kilogram, up over 130% since early 2025. Overseas tungsten APT holds above $3,300 per mtu, nearly quadruple Chinese domestic levels. The Democrats' midterm sweep introduces political uncertainty: a divided Congress could slow any bilateral agreement to extend the suspension. The hot CPI print compounds the difficulty — higher US rates and a stronger dollar may reduce appetite for concessions. Re-imposition would hit semiconductors, ammunition, hardened steel and EV battery supply chains.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Worst day in months · CPI hot at 0.4% MoM · Treasury 10Y jumped to 4.68% · Waller: 50bp 'should be considered'
desk.sum: Gold crashed 2.6% to $4,032 per ounce on Tuesday, its worst single-day decline in months, after October CPI came in hotter than expected. Headline CPI rose 0.4% MoM versus 0.3% consensus and core printed 0.3% versus 0.2%, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.68% and raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. Fed Governor Waller amplified the sell-off by suggesting a 50-basis-point hike at the December meeting 'should be considered.' The dollar strengthened on the rates repricing, adding further pressure. Gold's retreat from Tuesday morning's $4,095 level was swift, erasing the midterm-driven gains. Central bank buying continues at elevated levels but proved insufficient to absorb the CPI-driven selling. The next major catalyst is the November employment report on December 5.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Hit harder than gold on dual precious-industrial weakness · gold-silver ratio widened · CPI-driven selloff
desk.sum: Silver plunged 3.9% to $51.32 per ounce, underperforming gold as both its precious and industrial demand drivers weakened simultaneously. The hot CPI print hammered the precious-metal bid through higher yields and a stronger dollar, while the risk-off environment and hawkish Fed repricing weighed on industrial demand expectations. The gold-silver ratio widened as silver's higher beta amplified the move. Solar panel manufacturing demand provides a structural floor, but near-term sentiment is dominated by the rates outlook. The December FOMC meeting — with Waller floating a 50bp hike — is the key catalyst for the precious metals complex.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $86.04 · Iran deal expands to nuclear scope · 3.67% enrichment cap · Trump: war 'effectively over' · Brent down 17%+ in 8 sessions
desk.sum: Brent crude settled at $91.49 per barrel on Tuesday, down 1.2%, extending its collapse to over 17% from recent highs. WTI fell to $86.04. The Iran deal talks expanded dramatically: the framework now includes a 3.67% uranium enrichment cap, IAEA inspections and up to $9 billion in sanctions relief, far broader than Monday's Hormuz-only proposal. President Trump told reporters the war is 'effectively over.' OPEC output rose 1.38 million bpd in October; JPMorgan estimates a 1.4 million bpd global surplus. However, physical Gulf supply remains tight — Murban crude near $99 — and Eurasia Group still pegs peace odds at just 10%. Cabinet members remain divided on the deal. The hot CPI print added a modest headwind by strengthening the dollar.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME $13,780/t · hot CPI + higher yields pressure industrials · dollar strength reverses midterm gains
desk.sum: Copper fell 1.19% to $6.25 per pound ($13,780 per tonne LME 3M), as the hot CPI print and resulting dollar strength reversed midterm-driven gains. Higher Treasury yields at 4.68% weighed broadly on industrial metals. Chilean supply remains constrained and Chinese smelter-grade concentrate treatment charges are at multi-year lows. SMM reports Chinese copper stocks at approximately 60,000 mt, roughly 140,000 mt below last year. The hawkish Fed repricing — with Waller floating a 50bp hike — could further pressure copper if the dollar rally extends. China's economic outlook remains the key demand variable.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Down from $152 Oct high · broader energy complex under pressure · LNG tightness still provides floor
desk.sum: Newcastle coal dropped 2% to $138 per tonne, extending its decline from the $152 October high as the broader energy complex remained under pressure. Oil's continued slide and the prospect of Hormuz reopening weighed on energy prices broadly. However, coal retains support from continued LNG tightness — QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through year-end, keeping alternative fuel demand elevated. The hot CPI print and hawkish Fed stance introduce an additional headwind through dollar strength. If the Iran deal materialises and Hormuz reopens, both coal and LNG prices could face significant downside as energy supply normalises.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Gave back recent gains · CPI-driven precious metals rout · WPIC supply deficit still supportive longer term
desk.sum: Platinum fell an estimated 2.3% to approximately $1,510 per ounce, giving back recent gains in the CPI-driven precious metals rout. The hot inflation print and surging Treasury yields pressured all precious metals, with platinum's industrial demand profile offering limited shelter. The WPIC supply deficit narrative and hydrogen electrolysis growth continue to underpin the longer-term outlook. Platinum's decline was roughly in line with gold, reflecting the broad-based nature of the sell-off rather than platinum-specific weakness. Lower oil prices reduce mining energy costs but also signal weaker industrial demand.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Testing $1,000 support again · CPI selloff compounds EV transition headwind · Nornickel maintenance supports
desk.sum: Palladium fell approximately 2% to $1,021 per ounce, testing the $1,000 psychological support level again. The hot CPI selloff compounded the ongoing structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter. Nornickel's plant overhaul provides near-term supply support. The dollar's CPI-driven strength adds further pressure. If palladium breaks below $1,000, it could trigger technical selling. The broader precious metals complex is under pressure from the hawkish Fed repricing, with Waller's 50bp suggestion raising the bar for any dovish pivot.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: Iran deal expands to nuclear scope · 3.67% enrichment cap · IAEA inspections · up to $9B relief · attacks continue · Trump: 'effectively over'
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz risk level remains critical despite dramatic diplomatic progress. Iran deal talks expanded beyond the original Hormuz reopening proposal to include nuclear dimensions: a 3.67% uranium enrichment cap, IAEA inspections and up to $9 billion in sanctions relief. President Trump told reporters the war is 'effectively over.' However, cabinet members remain divided, with Rubio calling earlier demands 'outrageous and ridiculous.' Despite the diplomatic track, four attacks occurred between November 1 and 3 and the Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Aramco's Riyadh offices. Traffic through the strait remains 'substantially reduced' to single-digit to low-double-digit transits per day. Iraq's lane via Oman is operational. Eurasia Group still pegs peace odds at just 10%, but the nuclear dimension is new and could accelerate negotiations.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: WASDE cut yield to 179.6 from 181.2 — below all estimates · ending stocks trimmed · managed money was short
desk.sum: December corn rallied 1.35% to settle at 449¢ per bushel after the USDA's November WASDE report delivered a bullish surprise. The US corn yield forecast was cut to 179.6 bushels per acre from 181.2 in October, below the lowest analyst estimate, reflecting late-season dryness in portions of the western Corn Belt. Ending stocks were trimmed deeper than expected, tightening the 2026/27 supply outlook. Managed money was positioned net short going into the report, amplifying the upside reaction. The bullish WASDE partially offset the risk-off mood from the hot CPI print. Corn has now recovered from its recent lows below 443¢.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Gained on broader grains bid · Black Sea export corridors still tight · Russian exports at half normal volume
desk.sum: December wheat gained 0.80% to settle at 593¢ per bushel (CBOT settle 592.75¢), supported by the broader grains rally triggered by the bullish WASDE report. While the WASDE's primary surprise was in corn, wheat benefited from sympathetic buying and continued tightness in Black Sea export corridors. Russian wheat exports are running at about half their normal volume. Abu Dhabi talks could restart stalled grain shipments, which would be a significant bearish catalyst. The hot CPI and stronger dollar provided a mild headwind. Wheat remains well above its mid-October lows but has shed significant value over the past month.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: WASDE tightened balance sheet · strongest grains performer on the day · Chinese buying still muted
desk.sum: January soybeans surged 2.51% to 1,225¢ per bushel (CBOT settle 1,224.50¢), the strongest performer in the grains complex after the WASDE report also tightened the soybean balance sheet. The upside surprised given that analysts had expected the USDA to raise its US soybean harvest forecast. Chinese buying interest remains muted, and the stronger dollar after the hot CPI print weighs on US export competitiveness. However, the WASDE-driven short covering was sufficient to power the rally. Global soybean demand fundamentals remain supportive heading into the South American planting season.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $2,040 · spot ETF outflows $1.3B second consecutive week · Fear & Greed at 30 · hot CPI adds rate headwind
desk.sum: Bitcoin slipped to approximately $73,500, down 0.8%, as the hot CPI print reinforced the hawkish rates outlook that has been weighing on risk assets. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows reached $1.3 billion for a second consecutive week — persistent institutional selling that continues to pressure prices. Ethereum dropped to $2,040, underperforming BTC with the ETH/BTC ratio near multi-week lows. The Fear and Greed Index fell to 30 (Fear). Fed Governor Waller's suggestion of a 50bp December hike is a fresh headwind for crypto, which tends to underperform in rising-rate environments. The Democrats' midterm sweep has also raised regulatory uncertainty for crypto-friendly legislation.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM low-$34s · TTF ~$34 · HH $3.02 · QatarEnergy force majeure extends · Iran nuclear deal could accelerate Hormuz reopening
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) holds in the low-$34 range per MMBtu for December delivery. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping about 5 bcm of supply offline. EU storage sits at approximately 74.7%, roughly 17% below the five-year average ahead of winter. Henry Hub firmed to $3.02. The expansion of Iran deal talks to include nuclear dimensions — a 3.67% enrichment cap and IAEA inspections — increases the probability that Hormuz could reopen, which would be a significant bearish catalyst for LNG as Qatari cargoes resume. Until then, the approaching Northern Hemisphere winter supports prices.
desk.src: S&P Global · Global LNG Hub · OilPrice.com

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait $765 · Iran nuclear deal could unlock supply · Nov 27 export-control deadline 16 days
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. The Iran deal's expansion to nuclear dimensions is potentially significant for sulfur: a broader agreement that includes IAEA inspections and enrichment caps would increase the odds of Hormuz reopening, allowing Middle Eastern sulfur shipments to resume and easing the acute supply squeeze. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). However, with cabinet opposition and continued attacks, relief is not imminent. Chinese domestic sulfur holds near 7,200 yuan per tonne. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 16 days away.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · demand firm for 2026
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367 per tonne, largely unchanged. BPC's India contract remains approximately $35 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Potash demand remains firm through 2026. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. The bullish WASDE corn report supports the demand outlook for fertilisers heading into the 2027 planting season. The hot CPI and stronger dollar have limited direct impact on potash pricing.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 16 days to Nov 27 deadline · Document No. 46 suspension expiring · market flat after Oct pullback from ¥100k+
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne, flat after an October pullback from the August high above 100,000 yuan. The critical near-term catalyst is the November 27 deadline — now 16 days away — when the suspension of China's export prohibition on antimony, gallium, germanium and superhard materials expires. Democrats' midterm sweep introduces political uncertainty around any bilateral extension, and the hot CPI has further complicated the macro backdrop. Re-imposition would tighten supply for ammunition, flame retardants and semiconductor manufacturing.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 16 days to Nov 27 deadline · China 98% of supply · midterms + hot CPI complicate extension
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, up over 130% since early 2025. The November 27 deadline is now 16 days away. The Democrats' midterm victory and the resulting political gridlock could complicate any bilateral agreement to extend the Busan truce suspension. The hot CPI print and stronger dollar add to the difficult negotiating environment. China produces about 98% of global gallium. Western supply-chain development is advancing but timelines stretch beyond 2027. The semiconductor downturn adds demand uncertainty, but the strategic premium remains elevated.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Soft on weak steel demand · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ supply
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds near $5.02 per pound, soft as steel demand weakens amid the global risk-off environment. The hot CPI and resulting dollar strength add further headwinds for industrial metals. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. The November 27 export-control deadline could impact vanadium if superhard materials restrictions are re-imposed.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Near 4-month low · ICE inventories at 2.5-yr high · mid-crop could fall 42–50% · Harmattan risk ahead
desk.sum: ICE cocoa trades near $4,700 per tonne, extending its slide toward a four-month low. Rising ICE warehouse inventories — now at a 2.5-year high — continue to pressure prices in the near term. However, the longer-term supply outlook remains concerning: irregular October rainfall in Ivory Coast, linked to El Niño, threatens flowering, and Reuters projects the 2026/27 mid-crop could fall 42–50% to 300,000–350,000 tonnes. Traders also fear Harmattan winds in December–January. StoneX projects 2026/27 global output could fall 9.6%, potentially turning the current surplus into a deficit. The stronger dollar after the hot CPI adds an additional headwind.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: DRC quotas 96,600 t/yr · Asian market remains pressured in Q4 · NMC-to-LFP shift continues
desk.sum: Cobalt holds at approximately $33,525 per tonne, under pressure. The Asian cobalt market is expected to remain pressured in Q4 amid lackluster demand. The DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027. The EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce cobalt intensity. The hot CPI and rising rate expectations add headwinds for commodities that rely on growth-sensitive demand.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Below ¥95k — near one-year low · Nov production to rise 35% MoM · supply overwhelms demand
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures remain near ¥92,000 per tonne, near a one-year low. Mysteel projects Chinese lithium carbonate production will rise 35% month-on-month in November as spodumene-based output expands — a significant bearish signal. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Downstream buyers remain cautious, purchasing mainly for rigid needs. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. The hawkish CPI and stronger dollar compound the bearish environment for lithium.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · auto demand solid
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), in a range-bound pattern. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. Oil's continued decline reduces synthetic rubber production costs, which could cap natural rubber upside. The stronger dollar post-CPI is a mild headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot mid-$80s · long-term contracts near $96–99/lb · AI-driven demand · Kazakhstan shortfalls
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds near $86 per pound U₃O₈, stabilised in the mid-$80s. Long-term contract prices continue to rise, with record US contract prices near $99 per pound — close to the $100 milestone — as utilities lock in supply amid energy security concerns. Over 440 reactors operate worldwide with 60 or more under construction. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver. Kazakhstan (43% of mine output) faces production shortfalls from acid supply constraints. The hot CPI and rising yields have limited direct impact on the uranium market, which trades primarily on supply-demand fundamentals and energy policy.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: CREA November index fell to 254.7 · ex-China FOB $109–121/kg · Lynas shutdown adds supply risk
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $72 per kilogram domestically in China, while ex-China FOB prices sit at $109–121/kg. The China Rare Earth Industry Association's November index fell to 254.7, extending October's weakness. Lynas' Malaysian plant is undergoing a one-month maintenance shutdown and its Kalgoorlie plant is halting for power grid upgrades, putting December-quarter ex-China output under pressure. Heavy rare earths (dysprosium, terbium) remain elevated in Western markets. The November 27 deadline adds further supply-chain risk for rare earth processing.

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · CIF China flat · steel demand stable
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, with minor fluctuations. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The hot CPI and stronger dollar are modest headwinds. High-purity manganese sulfate for EV batteries is an emerging demand driver, though the lithium carbonate price decline reduces the urgency of battery chemistry diversification.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Down on CPI-driven dollar strength · Indonesia 67% mine · surplus persists
desk.sum: LME nickel fell 1.26% to $16,085 per tonne, pressured by the hot CPI print and resulting dollar strength. Nickel's surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. The hawkish Fed repricing — with Waller floating a 50bp hike — weighs on industrial metals through higher yields and a stronger dollar. Chinese smelter maintenance provides short-term tightness. The November 27 export-control deadline could impact nickel-adjacent supply chains if China re-imposes restrictions.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Edged up on supply tightness · LME stocks near 4,000 mt · Myanmar ban still constraining
desk.sum: LME tin edged up 0.24% to $46,313 per tonne, bucking the broader base metals decline on continued supply tightness. LME inventory holds near 4,000 mt — low for the year — providing a floor. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. Tin's outperformance on a broadly weak day for metals underscores its supply-driven fundamentals. The hot CPI and stronger dollar capped gains, preventing a more meaningful recovery toward the November 3 high of $48,225.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: TCs deeply negative · LME stocks down ~64% YTD to ~146,000 mt · smelter cuts continue
desk.sum: LME zinc fell 0.72% to $3,709 per tonne, pressured by the hot CPI and stronger dollar. Treatment charges remain deeply negative. LME inventories have fallen approximately 64% year-to-date to around 146,000 mt. Several Chinese and European smelters have cut output. The fundamental picture remains tight despite the broader risk-off environment weighing on base metals. The hawkish rates repricing adds near-term headwinds, but the structural supply deficit continues to provide a floor.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Overseas APT $3,300+ · China domestic APT ¥550k/t · Western prices 3–4x China · 16 days to Nov 27
desk.sum: Overseas APT holds above $3,300 per mtu, with Western prices running roughly three to four times Chinese domestic levels. Domestic APT remains at 550,000 yuan per tonne. The tungsten market continues to 'fragment' as Chinese domestic prices decouple from export prices. China's export controls on tungsten processing technology have created a severe non-Chinese supply crisis. The November 27 Busan truce deadline — now 16 days away — remains the critical uncertainty. Democrats' midterm sweep and the hot CPI further complicate the bilateral negotiating environment.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · Iran nuclear deal could accelerate repair timeline
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. The Iran deal's expansion to nuclear dimensions is relevant for helium: a comprehensive agreement that includes enrichment caps and IAEA inspections would increase the probability of broader conflict de-escalation, potentially accelerating repair work on Qatar's Ras Laffan facilities — currently estimated at 3–5 years. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. Commercial inventories remain at their lowest since 2008. Semiconductor fabs, MRI machines and space launch consume most demand.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · WASDE bullish for fertiliser demand
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. The bullish WASDE report — with its corn yield cut and tighter grain balance sheets — is supportive for fertiliser demand heading into the 2027 planting season. If the expanded Iran deal materialises and Middle Eastern sulfur supply resumes, phosphate producers could see significant cost relief.
